body:
Why international cooperation is necessary

Digital communication and online offences do not always remain within one country's borders. A person in India may encounter a fraudulent account operated from another country. A digital service used by Indian citizens may store relevant information in more than one jurisdiction. Countries therefore need lawful arrangements to exchange information, coordinate incident response and seek assistance in investigations.

International cooperation has several different forms. Technical cooperation helps cybersecurity agencies share alerts and respond to incidents. Law-enforcement cooperation assists authorities dealing with offences and suspects across borders. Legal cooperation provides procedures through which one country may seek evidence or other assistance from another.

Important international mechanisms

Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties

Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) provide formal arrangements for one country to request specified legal assistance from another in criminal matters. Depending on the treaty and domestic law, assistance may concern evidence, records or other investigative steps.

An MLAT is not a general permission for investigators to ignore another country's laws. Requests must proceed through the applicable legal framework and designated authorities.

INTERPOL and law-enforcement cooperation

INTERPOL facilitates international police cooperation and information exchange. It is not a world police force that ordinarily replaces national police or directly investigates every offence inside member countries. Indian investigating agencies continue to act under Indian law and cooperate internationally through the appropriate channels.

Cooperation among cybersecurity agencies

National computer emergency response teams can exchange information about incidents, alerts and protective measures through authorised cooperation arrangements. This differs from seeking evidence for criminal prosecution. A single cross-border event may require both forms of cooperation.

United Nations Convention against Cybercrime

The United Nations Convention against Cybercrime was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 24 December 2024. It addresses international cooperation concerning specified crimes involving information and communication technology systems and the sharing of electronic evidence relating to serious crimes.

The Convention opened for signature in Hanoi on 25–26 October 2025, followed by a further period for signature at United Nations Headquarters. India signed the Convention on 25 September 2026.

Under Article 65(1), the Convention enters into force on the 90th day after the deposit of the 40th instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession, with instruments deposited by regional economic integration organisations not counted in addition to those deposited by their member States. Signing a convention is therefore not the same as ratifying it, and adoption is not the same as entry into force.

Status on 16 November 2026: According to the United Nations Treaty Collection, the Convention had 96 signatories and 3 parties and was not yet in force. India was listed as a signatory but not as a party. These figures describe the status at this date and may change later.

Foreign influence and international cooperation are different issues

Foreign information manipulation concerns attempts to deceive or improperly influence the information environment. International cooperation concerns legitimate arrangements between countries and institutions. One foreign-origin message is not necessarily interference, just as international information sharing by law-enforcement agencies is not an influence operation.

When a suspected foreign-linked disinformation campaign is reported, its authenticity, coordination and origin need separate assessment. Where conduct also constitutes a criminal offence, competent authorities may seek international assistance. Attribution to a foreign government should not be assumed merely because an online account appears to operate from another country.

Matching the problem to the responsible institution

Accurate answers to prelims questions often depend on identifying the main nature of the problem before selecting the relevant law or institution.

  • Suspected false public announcement: Verify the original source and context; use relevant platform-reporting arrangements where appropriate.
  • Financial cyberfraud affecting a citizen: Use 1930 or the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with investigation handled by the competent police agency.
  • Reportable cybersecurity incident at an organisation: Apply the relevant CERT-In directions and sector-specific reporting arrangements.
  • Threat to qualifying critical information infrastructure: NCIIPC has the specialised national protection mandate; relevant incident-response agencies may also coordinate.
  • Cyber incident in the electricity sector: CSIRT-Power provides sectoral coordination and support alongside other competent agencies.
  • Issue concerning personal-data processing: Examine the DPDP framework, its commencement status and the functions legally assigned to the Data Protection Board.
  • Cross-border criminal evidence: International police and legal cooperation mechanisms may be relevant.

One incident may involve several institutions without making their roles identical. A fraudulent account can require platform action and police investigation. A compromised electricity utility can require national incident coordination, sectoral support and critical-infrastructure protection. Each authority acts within its own legal or institutional mandate.

Prelims focus

  • MLATs concern formal cross-border legal assistance in criminal matters.
  • INTERPOL facilitates police cooperation; it does not replace national police.
  • The UN Convention against Cybercrime was adopted on 24 December 2024.
  • India signed the Convention on 25 September 2026.
  • Article 65(1) provides for entry into force 90 days after the 40th qualifying instrument is deposited.
  • Trap: The Convention was not in force on 16 November 2026, and India's signature did not amount to ratification.
